This page is written according to the U.S. O*NET-SOC 17-2111.02 “Fire-Prevention and Protection Engineers” (the fixed index assigns this asset the Chinese occupational name for this occupation, and the body text follows that official occupational scope); this occupation is a detailed occupation under 17-2111.00 “Health and Safety Engineers, Except Mining Safety Engineers and Inspectors”. Even within fire prevention and protection engineering, the differences are large: building fire protection system design and performance-based evaluation, fire facility selection and construction drawing review, fire risk analysis for industrial and storage facilities, fire and smoke simulation calculations, component and system testing and verification, code and standard development, and engineering analysis for insurance and accident investigation. Before comparing positions or development paths, first check: professional engineer registration and sealing requirements, the applicable code and standard versions, design responsibility and review procedures, the safety and health requirements for site work, and whether statutory fire review and acceptance procedures are involved.

Validate with one paper exercise: you are given a completely fictitious building fire protection design assignment (building use and height, floor plan and evacuation layout, structure and finish materials, fire water and alarm system conditions, applicable fire protection code clauses, and submission and acceptance milestones). You are asked to write out the fire compartmentation and evacuation scheme, the fire system selection and design parameters, the fire protection component and material requirements, the calculations and tests that need to be done, and which conclusions must be confirmed by a professional engineer or the competent department; mark which determinations require the original code text or approval.

Signals worth considering more: willingness to study codes and calculation methods over the long term, ability to write one's own calculations and conclusions into reviewable documents, and willingness to communicate repeatedly with design and construction units and the competent department. Signals requiring caution: unwillingness to do calculations and read drawings closely, avoidance of code clauses and signing of responsibility, and treating the experience of a single project as a general rule.
This card is a career exploration reference and does not constitute hiring, ability scoring, engineering design, or safety conclusions.

First judge whether you are willing to make code study and engineering calculation a long-term career: it requires doing fire protection design and compliance review according to codes, writing calculations and determinations into reviewable documents, and bearing engineering responsibility for the design results; validate with the paper exercise and seven-day task on this page.

The work of fire prevention and protection engineers revolves around the cycle of “requirements confirmation—scheme design—calculation and testing—review and delivery—construction support”: first confirm the use, size, and hazard characteristics of the building or facility and collect the applicable fire protection codes and standards; then review the building drawings and floor layout to determine the fire compartmentation, evacuation exits, fire resistance and finish materials, and the requirements for fire water, alarm, and suppression systems; then carry out fire system design, hydraulic and smoke calculations, and component and system testing and verification, using simulation tools to evaluate performance-based schemes where necessary; write design statements, compliance review opinions, and fire technical reports and support submission and competent department approval; during construction, support installation, commissioning, and acceptance and handle design changes; at the same time participate in code and standard revisions, conduct fire cause research, and provide fire technical consulting and training to building design and construction personnel. The emphasis differs greatly by direction: building fire protection design stresses code application and system selection, industrial fire protection stresses hazard source analysis and explosion protection, codes and review stress compliance judgment and document quality, and research and testing stress test design and data analysis.

U.S. O*NET-SOC 17-2111.02 “Fire-Prevention and Protection Engineers”: research the causes of fires, determine fire prevention methods, and design or recommend materials and equipment such as structural components and fire detection devices to help organizations protect lives and property from fire, explosion, and related hazards.

entries.answer: This page is written according to the U.S. O*NET-SOC 17-2111.02 “Fire-Prevention and Protection Engineers” (the fixed index assigns this asset the Chinese occupational name for this occupation): research the causes of fires, determine fire prevention methods, and design or recommend materials and equipment such as structural components and fire detection devices to help organizations protect lives and property from fire, explosion, and related hazards. Specifically this includes: reviewing building drawings and verifying fire code compliance; designing fire detection devices, alarm systems, and suppression devices; evaluating fire protection conditions such as water supply, evacuation exits, and building materials; determining the fire protection requirements for structural components and finish materials; testing and verifying components and equipment such as fire doors and smoke control systems; preparing fire technical reports and review opinions; providing fire technical consulting and training to architects, construction personnel, and the competent department; and participating in fire cause research and code and standard revisions.
entries.question: What do Fire-Prevention and Protection Engineers mainly do?

entries.answer: Outputs and authority differ: this occupation produces fire system design, code compliance review, and fire risk research and is an engineering occupation; fire inspectors and investigators focus on site inspection, permits, and fire cause investigation and belong to the enforcement and investigation category; firefighters focus on firefighting, rescue, and emergency response; building and construction inspectors focus on building structure and construction quality inspection; occupational health and safety specialists focus on workplace hazard identification and safety management; environmental engineers focus on pollution control and environmental compliance; and health and safety engineers (17-2111.00, the parent occupation) have a broader scope covering general workplace safety and health engineering design, of which this occupation is the fire prevention detailed direction.
entries.question: How does it differ from fire inspectors and investigators and health and safety engineers?

entries.answer: U.S. O*NET-SOC 17-2111.02 “Fire-Prevention and Protection Engineers” is a detailed occupation under 17-2111.00 “Health and Safety Engineers, Except Mining Safety Engineers and Inspectors”. Definition notes: this detailed occupation has no separate BLS wage and employment series, and the wages presented on the O*NET page (2025 median hourly wage $55.36, median annual wage $115,160; the 10th, 25th, 75th, and 90th percentiles about 68,420, 90,930, 142,980, and 171,250 USD / year respectively), employment (about 23,800 in 2024), growth (average 3% to 4% for 2024—2034), and job openings (about 1,500 per year) are all on the parent occupation 17-2111.00 definition, marked at each occurrence on this page and not treated as separately listed values for this detailed occupation. BLS OOH is also published by parent occupation (2025 median annual wage $115,160, 22,300 employed, 5% growth for 2025—2035, and about 1,200 average annual openings). The education survey has published the leading items (bachelor's degree 85%, associate or other two-year degree 4%, post-baccalaureate certificate 4%), the remaining items are not published, and this page does not fill them in.
entries.question: What are the U.S. statistical definitions and profile completeness (important)?

entries.answer: O*NET lists this occupation as Job Zone Four (requiring considerable preparation, SVP 7.0 to <8.0). Work context shows that 69% work more than 40 hours per week; 96% use email every day, 71% make telephone calls every day, and 44% have face-to-face discussions every day; 54% are in contact with others most of the time; 46% work indoors in an environmentally controlled setting every day; 50% consider teamwork very important; decision freedom is some freedom for 58%; 36% write letters and memos every day; 42% consider precision or high accuracy very important; 48% sit more than half the time; 38% consider dealing with external customers or the public very important; time pressure is once a month or more but not every week for 54%; 31% have high responsibility for the health and safety of others; competitiveness is medium competition for 77%. The work is mainly drawing review and calculation in the office, and also requires surveys and testing at construction sites and existing buildings.
entries.question: What are the daily work context and preparation level like?

entries.answer: The more accurate judgment is that steps such as code clause searching, drawing and design document comparison, calculation drafts and report drafting, and testing data organization will be taken over by tools, and the occupation as a whole will mainly see augmentation and an upward shift in the center of responsibility. The ILO 2023 study shows that task exposure varies greatly across occupations, that the share of highly exposed tasks in managerial and professional occupations is relatively low, and that technical feasibility does not mean agencies have already adopted it; scheme choices, parameter assumptions, compliance judgments, and engineering signing responsibility must be borne by registered engineers, so the conclusion is that the way of working will change, not that the occupation as a whole will be replaced.

BLS OOH publishes for the same parent occupation a 2025 median annual wage of $115,160 (hourly $55.36). The median is the midpoint of the wage distribution of the employed, not a starting wage; OEWS is on an employed-person definition, and BLS has not published a readable figure for this occupation's industry-specific wages. Personal income also depends on professional registration, industry, and project type.

entries.answer: O*NET lists this occupation as Job Zone Four (requiring considerable preparation, SVP 7.0 to <8.0); the O*NET summary page lists the education level required of new employees: bachelor's degree 85%, associate or other two-year degree 4%, and post-baccalaureate certificate 4%, with the remaining items unpublished and not filled in by this page. BLS indicates that the typical entry-level education for the parent occupation is a bachelor's degree, usually with no related work experience or on-the-job training required, and recommends gaining practical experience through internships or cooperative education; professional engineer qualification usually requires passing a practice examination on the basis of an accredited degree and meeting practical experience requirements. In mainland China, a fire protection engineering or safety engineering degree plus practice qualifications such as registered fire engineer and project experience is commonly required; the specifics are subject to the job posting and local regulations.
entries.question: What education and qualifications are required?

entries.answer: Signing and approval of engineering design documents usually requires a professional engineer or fire protection specialty practice qualification and is limited by the employer's design qualifications and practice scope; fire design review, testing, and acceptance steps may also require corresponding qualifications and personnel conditions. These requirements must be verified against the original text of the target employer, the competent department, and local regulations; this page does not provide legal or compliance advice and does not equate a certificate with engineering design and judgment ability.
entries.question: What certificates or permits are required?

entries.answer: Technical responsibility for the fire protection design and the basis of the calculations rest with the personnel carrying them out; the compliance conclusions of engineering design, fire acceptance conclusions, and accident determination must be made by professional engineers, the competent department, and statutory procedures. Design must be carried out according to the original text of the applicable codes and standards, the assumptions and applicable scope of calculations and models must be stated and reviewable, and project materials and owner information must be kept confidential according to contract and institutional rules; site work must be carried out in accordance with occupational safety and health requirements. When using tools, tool outputs do not constitute design documents or an approval basis, and matters beyond one's own registration discipline and practice scope must be assigned to a qualified professional engineer or professional body. This page does not replace building fire protection and fire technical standards, fire facility design and acceptance codes, hazardous materials and material fire protection regulations, engineering registration and practice management systems, or occupational safety and health requirements.

description.text: What Fire-Prevention and Protection Engineers do, how to enter the field, work boundaries, and development directions. Based on official O*NET and BLS occupational data (O*NET-SOC 17-2111.02); the wages and employment of this detailed occupation are presented by O*NET on the parent occupation 17-2111.00 definition and marked at each occurrence on the page, and mainland China can only use industry and job category average wages as proxies.

subject.name: Fire-Prevention and Protection Engineers
subject.summary: Research the causes of fires, determine fire prevention methods, and design or recommend materials and equipment such as structural components and fire detection devices to help organizations protect lives and property from fire, explosion, and related hazards: includes reviewing building drawings and verifying fire code compliance, designing fire detection and alarm systems and suppression devices, evaluating fire protection conditions such as water supply and evacuation exits, testing fire protection components and fire systems, preparing fire protection plans and technical reports, participating in revisions of codes and standards, and providing fire technical consulting and training to building design and construction personnel.
